articles.title: My dad died suddenly with no will. Am I morally obliged to share his estate with my estranged half-sibling? | Leading questions
articles.summary: It’s kind of you to wonder if you should change the way things were left, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But it’s possible his preference is already clear. My dad died suddenly earlier this year, with no will, and I am unsure as to how I should distribute the estate.
body: My dad was a very ethical person. While his death was unexpected, he had a sense it was coming. Around six months before he died, he arranged for the disposal of many personal effects. The lack of a will, given his self-discipline and preferences for forward planning, is odd.

My dad has two daughters from a previous relationship, who he was not in contact with until I was in my mid-30s. Their mum had remarried after separating from our dad, and her new husband had formally adopted both her girls. My dad was delighted to resume contact with one half-sister. Another, two years younger, wanted nothing to do with him and firmly disapproved of her sister’s choice to re-establish contact.

Some 10 years ago, I started my own family, relocated to remove myself from domestic abuse, and joined the league of parents of children with additional needs. My dad mentioned that he had a little money put aside that could go towards legal costs, should courts ever become involved in arrangements for my son.
points: It’s kind of you to wonder if you should change the way things were left, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith.
But it’s possible his preference is already clear.

articles.title: A sun goddess, hundreds of devotees – and polluted water: the Nigerian festival threatened by gold mining
articles.summary: Each year, people from across the world gather in a grove sacred to the Yoruba goddess Osun to be healed, conceive or realise their deepest wishes. But toxic lead, mercury and cyanide is leaching into the river.
body: 7Devotees in white clothing line the riverbank, praying as they carry offerings of fruit, kola nut and sacrificial animals in supplication to Osun, the Yoruba goddess of fertility, beauty and healing, whose carved form stands with arms outstretched a few metres away in the Osun River.
It is the final day of Nigeria’s annual Osun Osogbo festival in honour of the African deity, in a tradition that has existed for hundreds of years and draws people from across the diaspora.

Except this year the water was once again a discoloured brown. Until 2018, the river ran clear, but then mining several miles upstream began to pollute it, introducing heavy metals and sediment into the watercourse.

The river, named after the goddess, runs through the Osun-Osogbo sacred grove, a 75-hectare (185-acre) Unesco world heritage site since 2005. The water is believed to possess healing powers and women who have trouble conceiving, or people in search of promotion or prosperity, often come to pray at the riverbank; the water is drunk or used for bathing, depending on the “directions” of the goddess.
points: Each year, people from across the world gather in a grove sacred to the Yoruba goddess Osun to be healed, conceive or realise their deepest wishes.

articles.title: Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?
articles.summary: Relocation coincides with proposed laws that opponents say would entrench power of US tech billionaires in country. Dozens of protesters converged on Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week after a congressional session raised questions about the billionaire’s presence in the country.
body: In white masks, they held signs saying “Peter Thief” and “No to the Peter Thiel law” in front of the wrought-iron gates of the $12m (£8.9m) residence, which Thiel bought in April as he moved his family to Argentina.

There is broad unease at the tech magnate’s presence in the country. His move has been characterised as part of a plan to hedge against world war three: Argentina, agriculturally rich and deep in the southern hemisphere, might just be the ideal place for a tech billionaire to wait out the apocalypse.
But recent developments in the country suggest Thiel could have more pragmatic considerations.

Last week, Argentina’s chamber of deputies held a six-hour debate on a set of sweeping regulatory changes put forward by Javier Milei’s rightwing government shortly after Thiel moved to Buenos Aires. They invited Thiel, Milei and an official linked to Argentina’s intelligence services to answer questions.

articles.summary: As the 2026 Venice Film Festival kicks off this week, all eyes will be on the red carpet—with the likes of George and Amal Clooney, Claire Foy, and Robert Pattinson arriving in the Italian city. See all the best fashion from Venice Film Festival so far.
body: Red carpet lovers, it’s your lucky day: The 2026 Venice Film Festival has officially arrived.

The film roster for this year’s festival has plenty of buzzy projects to take in: Among them is Martin McDonagh’s Oscar-tipped black comedy Wild Horse Nine; Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime; a Robert Pattinson-led portrait of To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen; and Bunker, Florian Zeller’s marital drama starring Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem.

Better year, however, is what all of these A-listers will be wearing on the step and repeat for the splashy premieres. This is, after all, the festival that last year offered the first glimpses of new-era Chanel, Dior, Versace and Bottega Veneta before their respective runway debuts, and which has given us Lady Gaga’s feathered Valentino couture gown in 2018 and Zendaya’s wet-look Balmain dress in 2021, among other standout moments.

articles.title: Meet the Michelin Star Chef Now Making New York’s Hardest-to-Get Pies
articles.summary: In Queens, pastry chef Michelle Kogan—formerly of Nobu and Torrisi—is igniting a craze for her elevated, handmade pies. “Anything that creates something heartwarming and joyful is what I’m here to do,” she says.
body: Every weekend this summer, you could find New York pastry chef Michelle Kogan setting up shop at one of two outdoor markets: the Carroll Gardens market in Brooklyn, or the Sunnyside market in Queens. Inside her pop-up tents, Kogan—a Michelin Star chef—has been selling her handmade Mishie’s Sunnyside pies, and her presence at the local markets serves as a stark contrast to her impressive resumé, considering she has cut her teeth at institutions like Nobu, Morimoto, and Torrisi.

But this summer, without a buzzy restaurant scene or a team of sous-chefs to hide behind, Kogan decided to step out on her own: The past few months have revolved around just her, some delicious pies, and a singular vision to bring joy to her local communities. “I just started [selling the pies] renegade-style,” says Kogan. “At first, I felt a little embarrassed—doing it with my little shanty table.”

articles.title: Jennifer Lawrence Gets Real About Beauty and Aging
articles.summary: From oxygen mist to “baby Botox” and bike helmets, the Oscar winner (and Dior ambassador) gives Vogue a refreshingly unfiltered take on the state of 2026 beauty and wellness.
body: In sweatpants and embroidered memory-foam slippers, Jennifer Lawrence pads into the newly opened Dior Spa Cipriani at Hotel Cipriani, A Belmond Hotel, Venice. That in itself is a sight to behold, but as she sits down next to me, she easily opens a bottle of water that I had been struggling with moments before. Consider me doubly impressed.

Close up on a cream bouclé love seat, Lawrence really is keeping it spa-day light (she speaks “pee-pee-poo-poo” into my phone when I announce I’m recording), really is unfiltered (calls me “moneybags” for throwing out a moldy humidifier instead of cleaning it with vinegar), and really is making me laugh in that way other girls with older brothers always can. She wears no visible makeup and has no visible pores (not that there’s anything wrong with the ones you can see!), and her natural waves fall in a perfectly chill way over her plain white tee.
points: From oxygen mist to “baby Botox” and bike helmets, the Oscar winner (and Dior ambassador) gives Vogue a refreshingly unfiltered take on the state of 2026 beauty and wellness.

articles.title: The Berkshires Are a Cultural Hotspot—and the Time to Visit Is Now
articles.summary: Celebrated for its scenery and thriving cultural scene, there’s never been a better time to visit the Berkshires. Here, a curated list of places to visit on your next getaway to the mountains.
body: There are certain destinations we know we’ll visit some day, but for one reason or another, they sit on the back burner. Since moving to New York City over a decade ago, I knew my time with the Berkshires would eventually come. Earlier this summer, at long last, it finally did.

If you’re familiar with this highland region in western Massachusetts, it may have something to do with Edith Wharton, who famously relocated here in pursuit of “the real country.” Or Herman Melville, who wrote Moby Dick from a desk overlooking Mount Greylock, said to be the inspiration for his white whale. Or perhaps you’ve heard of Tanglewood and Jacob’s Pillow, prolific music and dance centers, respectively. If you’re an art lover, MASS MoCA is likely on your radar. Wellness enthusiast? The concentration of pioneering spas (like Canyon Ranch ) is notable. And for the leaf peepers, the area’s astonishing fall landscapes are probably on your bucket list.
